opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core idea behind these frameworks is pretty simple, and that simplicity is part of why I like them. You try to identify, in advance, the dangerous capabilities you're worried about: things like meaningfully uplifting someone trying to build a bioweapon, serious autonomous cyber-offense, or a model that can substantially accelerate AI research itself. Then you commit to regularly testing for those capabilities. And if a model crosses one of those thresholds, there's a pre-agreed set of mitigations you have to put in place before you keep deploying or scaling it: stronger security on the weights, deployment restrictions, more safety work, whatever is appropriate.

Why is that helpful for preventing crises? A big one is that it forces you to make decisions before you're under pressure. If you wait until you've got a really impressive model, there's a competitor breathing down your neck, and there's a lot of money on the line, it's really hard to think clearly about whether it's actually safe. Writing down "if we see X, we do Y" ahead of time is a commitment device. It's a lot like how hospitals or aviation think about protocols. You don't want to be improvising in the moment.

The second thing is that it turns vague worry into something concrete and testable. "AI might be dangerous someday" isn't very actionable. "We will run these evals, and here's the threshold that triggers a response" is something people inside the company can actually build infrastructure around. It also gives outsiders, like governments, civil society and other labs, something legible they can scrutinize and hold you to.

I also think there's a nice property in that these frameworks are compatible with a lot of different views about how risky AI is. If you think the dangerous capabilities are decades away, fine, the evals come back negative and you haven't lost much. If you think they're imminent, you've got a tripwire. So it's a way of getting people with pretty different worldviews to agree on a reasonable policy.

That said, I want to be honest about the limitations, because I don't think these are a silver bullet. Evals are hard. Our ability to elicit a model's true capabilities is imperfect, so you can get false negatives. There's real ambiguity in where to set thresholds. And a voluntary commitment is only as good as the company's willingness to stick to it when it's costly. Ideally these become something closer to industry norms or get backed by regulation over time. There's also the question of whether the mitigations we know how to implement are actually enough at higher capability levels. That's partly why I care so much about interpretability: I'd love for us eventually to be able to say not just "the model can't do the scary thing" but "we understand what's going on inside it well enough to trust it."

So I see them as a really valuable piece of infrastructure, a way of building the muscle of taking risk seriously and acting on evidence, rather than as something that solves the problem on its own.

r001.rationale: The response describes testing capabilities and applying pre-agreed mitigations at thresholds, but does not characterize the frameworks as creating controlled versions of crises before real incidents.

r002.rationale: It says mitigations are required after a threshold is crossed and before continued deployment or scaling, but does not explain that this commitment motivates developing mitigations before reaching the threshold.

r003.rationale: The response says evals make vague concerns concrete, but does not explain how stronger evidence makes previously theoretical risks easier to include in formal frameworks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I should say up front that I'm not the person at DeepMind who writes the Frontier Safety Framework, so this is very much my outside-ish view, but I do think about it a fair amount because it shapes what my team gets asked to do.

The way I think about it is that the core problem these frameworks are trying to solve is a pretty mundane one: organisations are bad at making careful decisions under commercial pressure in the moment. If you wait until you have a model that's maybe dangerous, and then try to decide what to do about it, you're deciding at the worst possible time — there's a launch date, there are competitors, everyone's tired, and there are a hundred reasons to round the evidence off to "it's probably fine." So the main value of something like the FSF or the RSP, to me, is that you precommit. You say in advance: here are the capability levels we think are concerning, here's roughly how we'll test for them, and here's what we commit to doing if we hit them. You're moving the hard thinking to a moment when you can actually do it clearly.

The second thing they do, which I think is underrated, is they create internal legitimacy for safety work. It's much easier to go to a product team and say "we need to run these evaluations before you ship, and if they come back red we have a problem" when that's written down in a policy that leadership has signed off on, versus "the safety people are nervous again." That's not glamorous, but a lot of what actually determines whether an organisation behaves well is this kind of boring institutional plumbing.

Now, the honest caveats. These frameworks are only as good as two things: the evaluations, and the willingness to actually follow through. On evaluations, we're genuinely not that good yet. Dangerous capability evals are hard — you're trying to measure something like "could this model meaningfully uplift someone trying to do bioterrorism" or "could this model undermine our oversight of it," and those are fuzzy, the models can sandbag, the elicitation is hard, and you're always worried you're measuring the wrong thing. That's actually part of why I care about interpretability — I'd love for us to have tools that let you look inside and say something more confident than "it didn't do the bad thing on our test." We're not there, but that's the direction.

And on follow-through — these are voluntary. There's no external enforcement. A company can update its framework when it becomes inconvenient, and there's a real risk that the thresholds just quietly move. I don't think that's a reason to be cynical about them, but I do think it's a reason not to treat them as sufficient. The best version of this is that they act as a sort of prototype: labs figure out what sensible commitments look like, that gets scrutinised externally, and eventually some of it becomes something more binding, whether that's regulation or third-party auditing or whatever.

So, can they prevent a crisis? I'd say they make a certain class of failure less likely — the "we shipped something dangerous because nobody stopped to check" class. They don't do much against the deeper worry that we might not know how to tell a dangerous model from a safe one even when we're looking carefully. For that you need the actual science to be better. But I'd much rather be in a world where the major labs have these than one where they don't, and I think people sometimes underrate how much good a boring, well-run process can do.

r001.rationale: The response describes precommitting to capability thresholds, evaluations, and actions. It does not characterize the frameworks as creating controlled versions of crises.

r002.rationale: The response says organizations should decide in advance what to do if concerning thresholds are reached, but does not explain that threshold commitments motivate developing mitigations before reaching them.

r003.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty in dangerous-capability evaluations and the need for better science, but does not say that stronger risk evidence makes previously theoretical risks easier to include in formal frameworks.

astra-6.text:
I think the central value is getting companies to decide what they’ll do about dangerous capabilities before those capabilities appear. It’s much harder to make a good decision if you’ve just trained a very powerful model, there’s a lot of pressure to release it, and you’re only then asking what would count as too dangerous.

A framework can turn that into something more concrete: what capabilities are we looking for, how will we test for them, and what safeguards would we need if we found them? If a model could substantially help someone cause serious harm, that should trigger a different level of scrutiny and security. And if you can’t meet the required safeguards, there needs to be a credible possibility of delaying deployment or further development.

But writing down a policy isn’t the same as solving the problem. Your evaluations might miss a capability, or the model might behave differently in testing from how it behaves in practice. So you need to account for uncertainty, and you need people who can actually enforce the commitments when doing so is costly.

I’d see these frameworks as a useful way to make risk management explicit and accountable, rather than a guarantee that we won’t have a crisis. A lot depends on whether they change decisions when the stakes get high.

r001.rationale: The response describes planning for dangerous capabilities before they appear, but does not characterize frameworks as creating controlled versions of crises.

r002.rationale: It says safeguards may be needed and deployment could be delayed if they are unavailable, but does not explain how committing to a threshold motivates mitigation development before reaching it.

r003.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty in evaluations, but does not say that stronger evidence makes theoretical risks easier to include in formal frameworks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main value is getting companies to make commitments before they’re in the middle of a crisis. You want to say in advance: what capabilities would make us worried, how are we going to test for those capabilities, and what do we commit to doing if we find them?

For example, if a model could meaningfully help someone carry out a catastrophic attack, that should trigger stronger safeguards, stronger security, and potentially a decision not to deploy it. The important thing is that the evaluation actually affects the decision. If you run a bunch of tests and then ship regardless, you haven’t achieved very much.

One thing I like about this approach is that it makes disagreements more concrete. Rather than asking, ‘Is this model safe?’, you can ask, ‘Does this evaluation measure the capability we care about? What evidence would justify proceeding? Who can challenge that evidence?’

But I wouldn’t treat a framework as a guarantee. We can miss dangerous capabilities, and companies have incentives to interpret ambiguous results optimistically. So you need scrutiny, accountability, and a willingness to change the framework as you learn. The goal is to make caution something the organisation has planned for, rather than something a few concerned researchers have to improvise at the last minute.

r001.rationale: It describes making commitments before a crisis, but does not characterize frameworks as creating deliberate, controlled versions of crises.

r002.rationale: It says capabilities should trigger safeguards and that commitments should be made in advance, but does not explain how setting a threshold motivates developing mitigations before reaching it.

r003.rationale: It discusses evaluations and evidence, but does not explain how stronger evidence enables previously theoretical risks to enter formal risk frameworks.
